title: Safe Browsing Basics
body:
Safe browsing basics are the small checks made before a link is followed or a page is trusted. A web address is the page's real name, while the words on a link are only a label, and the two can disagree. Learning to read the address, to notice lookalike spellings, and to pause before entering information stops many common tricks before any damage is done.

This matters because most everyday harm online starts with an ordinary click on a page that looked familiar.

The working method is address-and-link checking before clicking. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read the full address in the address bar, not only the link text
  2. Compare the domain with the address you already know for that service
  3. Treat unexpected links in messages as unverified until checked another way
  4. Look for misspellings, extra words, and odd endings in the domain
  5. Close the page and type the known address yourself when in doubt

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Known service address typed directly; OK :: Link text matches its real destination; OK :: Domain spelling matches the known service; OK :: Unexpected link treated as unverified; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. These checks reduce risk but do not prove a page is safe on their own, because a genuine page can still be compromised and a careful imitation can pass a quick glance. Combine address checks with up-to-date software and a habit of verifying requests through a second channel. A common mistake is trusting a page because its logo and layout look professional, since both are easy to copy. title: Strong Passphrases in Plain Language
body:
A strong passphrase is a long secret built from several ordinary words that only its owner would string together. Length is what makes guessing hard: each added word multiplies the work of guessing far more than a single tricky character does. A passphrase that can be remembered without writing it down is one that will actually be used, and a different passphrase for each important account means one leak does not open every door.

This is the single habit that most improves account safety for the least effort, because it works on every service.

The working method is passphrase building from memorable words. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Pick four or more unrelated words that form a picture you can remember
  2. Avoid names, dates, and phrases tied to public facts about you
  3. Use a different passphrase for email, banking, and work accounts
  4. Store passphrases in a password manager rather than in plain notes
  5. Change a passphrase promptly if the service reports it was exposed

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK len=28 min=20 :: four-word passphrase; TOO SHORT len=4 min=20 :: short password; OK len=31 min=20 :: long phrase; long enough: 2/3; VERDICT: REVIEW - short values need attention. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Passphrases do not protect an account on their own if the device is shared without a lock, or if a second factor is missing on an important account. Pair long unique passphrases with a second factor wherever it is offered, and treat email as the most important account of all, since it resets the others. A common mistake is reusing one clever passphrase everywhere, which turns a single leak into a total loss. title: Spotting Urgent-Message Pressure
body:
Urgent-message pressure is the tactic of rushing a reader so that checking is skipped. Messages that threaten closure, loss, or punishment within hours, that claim authority from a bank, a delivery firm, or a government office, and that demand an immediate click or code are built to create panic. Recognizing the pressure itself, rather than debating the message's details, is the defense: urgency is a reason to slow down, not to hurry.

Pressure works because it targets the helpful, obedient part of a person, and it works best on people who are tired or busy.

The working method is urgency-and-authority pressure recognition. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Pause and name the pressure: this message wants me to act now
  2. Check the claim through a channel you already trust, not the one given
  3. Never send a password or a one-time code in reply to an unsolicited message
  4. Ask a second person when a message claims to come from a boss or relative
  5. Report the message through the service's reporting tool

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: CHECK :: Message demands action within one hour; CHECK :: Sender asks for a code by reply; OK :: Claim checked through a trusted channel; OK :: Message reported, not answered; ok: 2/4; VERDICT: REVIEW - 2 item(s) need attention. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Not every urgent message is a trick: real services do send genuine warnings. The rule is not to ignore urgency but to verify it independently, and the record does not cover legal advice about any particular message or dispute. A common mistake is arguing with the sender or clicking to see what happens, since both confirm the address is active. title: Sharing Less Online
body:
Sharing less online is the habit of reviewing a post for what it reveals before it is published. A photo can reveal a location, a school, a workplace, or a daily routine, and a casual post can reveal travel plans, a child's activities, or a new purchase. Once published, a post can be copied and kept even after it is deleted, so the review must happen before sharing, not after.

Most regret about sharing comes not from one dramatic post but from small details that add up over time.

The working method is before-you-share review of posts. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read the post as a stranger would and list what it reveals
  2. Check the background of photos for signs, uniforms, and locations
  3. Remove location data and delay travel posts until after returning
  4. Ask every person in a photo before posting it
  5. Review who can see the post and narrow the audience when unsure

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Photo background checked for location clues; OK :: Travel post delayed until after return; OK :: Permission asked from everyone pictured; OK :: Audience narrowed before posting; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Sharing less is a personal choice, not a rule that fits every life: public figures, sellers, and community organizers may need to share more, and this record supports their choices with the same review, not with a ban on sharing. A common mistake is assuming that deleting a post removes every copy, since copies and screenshots persist. title: Public Wi-Fi Habits
body:
Public Wi-Fi habits are the rules for using networks in cafes, hotels, libraries, and airports, where the network itself cannot be trusted. On such a network, traffic that is not encrypted can be seen by others nearby, and a network name can be imitated by a nearby device. The safe habits are simple: prefer encrypted connections, avoid sensitive accounts on open networks, and use a trusted virtual private network when one is available.

People meet public networks exactly when they are traveling and distracted, which is when careful habits matter most.

The working method is safe use on networks you do not control. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Check that the site address uses an encrypted connection before signing in
  2. Avoid banking and account changes on a network with no password
  3. Turn off automatic connection to open networks on the device
  4. Forget public networks after use so the device does not rejoin silently
  5. Use a trusted private network service on networks you do not control

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Encrypted connection confirmed before sign-in; OK :: Sensitive account avoided on open network; OK :: Automatic open-network joining turned off; OK :: Public network forgotten after use; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Encrypted connections protect the content of a visit but do not hide which sites are visited from the network operator, and a private network service is only as trustworthy as its provider. The record does not recommend any particular provider. A common mistake is trusting a network because it asks for a password, since a shared password does not keep other users of that network from seeing unencrypted traffic. title: Reporting and Blocking
body:
Reporting and blocking are the two actions that turn an upsetting encounter into a record and a boundary. Blocking stops further contact from an account, while reporting tells the service that a rule may have been broken and creates a case it can act on. Preserving evidence first, by saving the message or taking a screenshot with its date and sender visible, means the report survives even if the sender deletes the original.

Many people skip reporting because it feels useless, yet reports are how services learn which accounts are harming many people at once.

The working method is reporting, blocking, and preserving evidence. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Save the message or screenshot with sender and date visible before blocking
  2. Block the account so no further contact arrives
  3. Report through the service's own tool, choosing the closest rule
  4. Tell a trusted person what happened and keep the evidence copy
  5. Follow up only if the service asks for more detail, and do not re-engage with the sender

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Evidence saved with sender and date visible; OK :: Account blocked; OK :: Report filed through the service tool; OK :: Trusted person told; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Reporting does not guarantee removal, and services differ in how they handle reports. Where harm is serious or threatening, reporting to the service is not a substitute for contacting local authorities or a trusted support organization, which this record does not replace. A common mistake is deleting the evidence in anger before reporting, which removes the very material the report needs. title: Reading Privacy Settings
body:
Reading privacy settings means walking through an account's settings section by section instead of accepting defaults at a glance. The important sections are usually who can see posts, who can contact you, what data is collected, what is shared with partners, and what advertising personalization is turned on. Defaults often favor broad sharing, so the walkthrough is where a user's real preferences get written into the account.

Defaults are choices made by someone else, and a walkthrough is how a user replaces them with their own.

The working method is privacy-settings walkthrough by section. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Open settings and read each section heading before changing anything
  2. Set post visibility and contact permissions to the narrowest comfortable level
  3. Turn off advertising personalization and partner sharing where the choice exists
  4. Review which apps and devices are connected to the account and remove the unused ones
  5. Repeat the walkthrough after major updates, which sometimes reset settings

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Post visibility reviewed; OK :: Contact permissions reviewed; OK :: Advertising personalization reviewed; OK :: Connected apps reviewed and pruned; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Settings differ between services and change over time, so this record teaches the walkthrough pattern rather than promising that any particular switch exists on any particular service. It does not cover the legal meaning of any privacy policy. A common mistake is changing one visible switch and assuming the whole account is private, since settings live in several sections. title: Safe Video and Chat Habits
body:
Safe video and chat habits cover live conversation, where words and images cannot be taken back once sent. The habits are: keep video calls to people you know or to verified rooms, keep the camera background free of identifying details, never share a screen that shows private information, and end a call that turns uncomfortable without explanation or apology. For group chats, the habits add: check who else is in the room before speaking openly.

Live conversation feels private, but a participant can record it, and a room can hold strangers behind silent names.

The working method is video-and-chat conduct and controls. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Check who is in the call or chat before sharing anything personal
  2. Keep the camera background plain and free of documents and signs
  3. Never share a screen showing mail, passwords, or private files
  4. End an uncomfortable call at once and block if needed
  5. Agree chat rules with a group before sensitive topics are discussed

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Room membership checked before sharing; OK :: Camera background free of identifying detail; OK :: Screen share checked before starting; OK :: Uncomfortable call ended without delay; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. These habits reduce risk but cannot make a live call fully private, because any participant may record it. Sensitive matters that must stay private belong in a channel whose recording and retention rules are understood by everyone involved. A common mistake is staying on an uncomfortable call to be polite, since politeness is exactly what the pressure relies on. title: Download Safety
body:
Download safety is the habit of checking a file before opening it, because a file can carry more than its name promises. The checks are: download only from the source you intended, be wary of files that arrive unasked, check the file type against what was expected, and let security software scan the file before it is opened. A document that asks to enable extra features on opening deserves particular suspicion.

Files feel passive, but opening one is an action that hands the file's contents to a program that may run its instructions.

The working method is download-and-attachment checking. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Download from the intended source, not from a link in an unsolicited message
  2. Compare the file type with what was expected before opening
  3. Let security software scan the file and wait for its result
  4. Refuse extra features or macros a document asks to enable
  5. Delete files that arrive unasked and were never requested

title: Account Recovery Readiness
body:
Account recovery readiness means setting up the ways back into an account before they are needed. The pieces are a recovery email and phone number that are still in use, backup codes stored somewhere safe and separate from the device, and a second factor that has a backup method. Recovery is a calm, ten-minute task when done in advance and a crisis when attempted during a lockout.

People discover their recovery options are stale at the worst moment: when the account is already locked.

The working method is recovery options set before lockout. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Confirm the recovery email and phone number are current and reachable
  2. Generate backup codes and store them away from the device, on paper if needed
  3. Add a second factor and record its backup method
  4. Test recovery once on a low-value account to learn the steps
  5. Review recovery options whenever a phone number or email changes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Recovery email current and reachable; OK :: Recovery phone current and reachable; OK :: Backup codes stored away from the device; OK :: Second factor has a backup method; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Recovery options are also a target: anyone who controls the recovery email or phone can often take the account, so recovery contacts must be guarded as carefully as passwords. This record does not cover recovery from identity theft, which needs the service's dedicated process. A common mistake is storing backup codes only on the device they unlock, which makes them useless exactly when they are needed. title: Helping Others Stay Safe
body:
Helping others stay safe is teaching digital safety in a way people can actually hear. The method is: start from one habit the person already cares about, show it on their own device, practice it together once, and leave a short written reminder. Shame is the enemy of this work: a person who feels judged for a mistake will hide the next one instead of asking for help early.

Safety spreads through families and workplaces person by person, and the teacher's tone decides whether the lesson lands.

The working method is teaching safety without shame. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ask what the person worries about and start from that concern
  2. Show the habit on their device, then let them do it while you watch
  3. Practice once together, including the reporting and blocking steps
  4. Leave a short written reminder in plain words
  5. Check back later and praise the habit, not the fear

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Lesson started from the learner's own concern; OK :: Habit practiced on the learner's device; OK :: Short written reminder left behind; OK :: Follow-up check arranged; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Teaching does not make the teacher responsible for another adult's choices, and it does not replace professional help where harm, threats, or financial loss are involved. The record teaches peer help, not counseling or legal advice. A common mistake is lecturing about every danger at once, which leaves people overwhelmed and changes nothing. title: Evaluating a New App or Service
body:
Evaluating a new app or service means reading what it asks for before it is installed, not after it has already collected data. The review covers: which permissions it requests and whether each one fits its job, what data its notice says it collects, whether it offers account deletion, and what other users report about its behavior. An app that asks for contacts, location, and microphone access to do a job needing none of them has failed the review.

Installation is the moment of maximum leverage, because permissions granted casually are rarely reviewed later.

The working method is permission-and-terms review before install. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every permission the app requests and ask whether its job needs each one
  2. Read the data-collection section of its notice, not only the headline promises
  3. Check whether the service offers account deletion and data export
  4. Search for independent reports of its behavior before installing
  5. Install, test with minimal data, and remove it if it asks for more than its job needs

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: PASS score=4 threshold=4 :: Permissions fit the app's job; PASS score=3 threshold=3 :: Data collection section read; PASS score=3 threshold=3 :: Deletion and export offered; PASS score=2 threshold=2 :: Independent reports checked; passing: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all scores at threshold. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. A review cannot see inside a service's servers, and a service can change its behavior after installation, so the review is a starting judgment, not a guarantee. Repeating the review after major updates is part of the habit, and this record does not offer legal interpretation of any terms of service. A common mistake is judging an app by its rating alone, since ratings measure popularity and polish, not data behavior. title: Handling a Suspected Compromise
body:
Handling a suspected compromise means acting in the right order when an account or device seems to be in someone else's hands. The order is: change the password from a clean device, revoke active sessions, turn on a second factor, check recent activity for changes, and warn contacts if messages were sent in your name. Panic helps no one, but delay helps the intruder, so the steps are practiced in advance and followed calmly.

The first hour after discovery decides how much damage is contained and how much spreads to contacts.

The working method is first steps after a suspected compromise. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Change the password from a device you trust, starting with email
  2. Revoke active sessions and signed-in devices for the account
  3. Turn on a second factor and record its backup method
  4. Review recent activity, messages sent, and settings changed
  5. Warn contacts if messages went out in your name and report the incident

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Password changed from a trusted device; OK :: Active sessions revoked; OK :: Second factor turned on; OK :: Recent activity reviewed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. These steps contain a typical account compromise but do not cover a fully compromised device, which may need professional cleaning or a fresh install, nor financial fraud, which needs the bank's and authorities' processes promptly. The record does not promise recovery of lost data or money. A common mistake is changing the password on the same compromised device and stopping there, leaving sessions and settings untouched. title: Digital Safety Plan for a Household
body:
A digital safety plan for a household is a short written agreement about devices, accounts, and what to do when something goes wrong. It names who manages the router, who holds backup codes, what the rules are for children and guests, and how the household responds to a suspicious message or a lost device. Writing it down matters because a plan remembered differently by each person is not a plan at all.

Households share devices, networks, and accounts, so one person's weak habit becomes everyone's risk.

The working method is household safety plan and roles. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every device, account, and shared password holder in the household
  2. Assign one person to router and update duties and one to backup-code keeping
  3. Write rules for children, guests, and shared devices in plain words
  4. Agree the response steps for a lost device and a suspicious message
  5. Review the plan together twice a year and after any move or new device

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Devices and accounts listed; OK :: Router and backup duties assigned; OK :: Rules for children and guests written; OK :: Response steps agreed; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. A plan helps a household that can agree on rules, but it cannot force agreement where trust is broken or control is being misused. Where a household member uses devices or accounts to control or harm another, this record's plan is not the right tool, and outside help should be sought. A common mistake is writing a plan once and never revisiting it, since devices, services, and children all change. title: Safety for Work and Personal Separation
body:
Separating work and personal life online means keeping work accounts, devices, and data apart from personal ones wherever possible. The separation protects both sides: a personal compromise does not hand over work data, and a work policy change does not lock a person out of their own photos and mail. Practical separation includes distinct accounts, distinct browsers or profiles, and never forwarding work material to a personal account to work on it at home.

Blending is convenient until the day one side is compromised, investigated, or closed, and then the other side falls with it.

The working method is separating work and personal accounts and devices. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use separate accounts for work and personal services, with separate passwords
  2. Use separate browser profiles or devices for work and personal use
  3. Never forward work material to a personal account
  4. Keep personal files off work devices and work files off personal devices
  5. Review the separation when changing jobs, since access must be handed back cleanly

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Separate work and personal accounts in use; OK :: Separate browser profiles or devices in use; OK :: No work material forwarded to personal accounts; OK :: Separation reviewed on job change; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Perfect separation is not always possible, especially for people whose employer provides only one device, and this record does not override any employer's policy. Where separation is impossible, the record's fallback is separate profiles and careful forwarding rules, not ignoring the risk. A common mistake is using one account for everything because it is easier, which makes every compromise total. title: Keeping Skills Current
body:
Keeping skills current means treating digital safety as a subject that changes, not a lesson finished once. New message tricks, new app permissions, and new device features arrive every year, and a habit learned five years ago may miss them. The maintenance routine is small: follow one trusted public safety source, re-read account settings twice a year, and practice one new habit each season, such as reviewing connected apps or testing account recovery.

Safety knowledge decays quietly, because nothing announces that a trusted habit has gone out of date.

The working method is staying current as threats change. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Follow one trusted public safety source and read its warnings
  2. Re-read privacy and security settings twice a year
  3. Practice one new habit each season, such as an app-permission review
  4. Teach one habit to someone else, which tests whether you still understand it
  5. Replace habits that no longer fit the devices and services you actually use

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Staying current does not mean chasing every warning: many warnings concern services or devices a person does not use. The skill is filtering for what applies to one's own accounts and devices, and this record does not track any particular threat landscape in real time. A common mistake is collecting safety tips without ever practicing one, since unpracticed knowledge fails under pressure.
